seasons.description: Clarkson’s first revival run moves from classical mythology and Cold War history through astronomy, Scottish landmarks and natural history, establishing a question ladder in which almost any corner of general knowledge can become suddenly expensive.

episodes.title: Goddess Of Victory
episodes.description: Mythology supplies the episode’s first memorable identity as a goddess of victory enters the question ladder. It is an appropriately grand opening for Clarkson’s revival: ancient knowledge, modern nerves and absolutely no safe subject area.

episodes.title: The Land Of Nod
episodes.description: A biblical turn of phrase gives this episode its wonderfully sleepy title, while the quiz keeps doing the opposite. Familiar words become traps, obscure knowledge suddenly matters, and Clarkson discovers that being host does not automatically make one useful.

episodes.title: Checkpoint Charlie
episodes.description: Cold War geography provides the standout image as Checkpoint Charlie appears among an eclectic run of questions. History, popular culture and deceptively simple general knowledge collide in the usual Millionaire manner: politely, then all at once.

episodes.title: Balearic Islands
episodes.description: The Mediterranean supplies the episode’s geographical detour with the Balearic Islands. What looks like a pleasant mental holiday quickly becomes another reminder that Millionaire can turn maps, names and everyday knowledge into surprisingly expensive uncertainties.

episodes.title: Heliocentric
episodes.description: Astronomy takes the spotlight with the heliocentric view of the universe. A single scientific adjective gives the episode its identity while the surrounding ladder ranges freely through the sort of knowledge everyone vaguely remembers until four answers appear.

episodes.title: Urquhart Castle
episodes.description: A Scottish landmark beside one of the world’s most famous lochs becomes the episode’s defining destination. The question set wanders through history and culture while Clarkson treats geographical certainty as the optional extra it so often is.

episodes.title: Ibex
episodes.description: A sure-footed mountain goat becomes the oddly perfect mascot for an episode built around intellectual footing. The questions hop between subjects with similar agility, while contestants discover that recognition and certainty are very different creatures.

seasons.description: The second run ranges from Greek mythology and maritime mystery to aviation, mountaineering, northern European geography, Monopoly, vocabulary and surveying, with each subject offering a fresh way to turn recognition into uncertainty.

episodes.title: Queen Of The Underworld
episodes.description: Greek mythology opens the new year in suitably dramatic fashion with the queen of the underworld. Gods, legends and general knowledge share the ladder, producing the familiar Millionaire problem: knowing the story is easier than trusting the answer.

episodes.title: The Mary Celeste
episodes.description: The Mary Celeste brings one of history’s great maritime mysteries into the hot seat. The rest of the quiz moves through equally varied territory, though few subjects can compete with an apparently abandoned ship for instant episode identity.

episodes.title: Dallas, Brett And Kane
episodes.description: Three names form the episode’s most peculiar little constellation: Dallas, Brett and Kane. It is exactly the kind of question detail Millionaire excels at making suddenly important, surrounded by a ladder that refuses to stay in one intellectual postcode.

episodes.title: Three Peaks Challenge
episodes.description: Britain’s Three Peaks Challenge gives the episode some literal elevation. Geography and endurance make a memorable stop on a ladder that otherwise climbs by knowledge rather than altitude, with every new question offering its own small summit.

episodes.title: Skagerrak And Kattegat
episodes.description: Skagerrak and Kattegat turn northern European geography into something that sounds almost invented. The paired waterways make an ideal Millionaire curiosity: distinctive, slightly intimidating, and just familiar enough to make doubt especially irritating.

episodes.title: London Monopoly Board
episodes.description: The London Monopoly board transforms a familiar game into a test of suspiciously specific memory. Streets, colours and cultural knowledge mingle in an episode where knowing something casually is repeatedly shown to be inferior to knowing it precisely.

episodes.title: Condor
episodes.description: A condor soars into the episode’s question set and gives it a clean, memorable identity. Natural history joins the usual mixture of culture and general knowledge, with the ladder proving that even familiar creatures can become awkward under studio lights.

episodes.title: Gurney Flap
episodes.description: Aerodynamics contributes the delightfully technical Gurney flap, a tiny device with a disproportionately good name. It epitomises the episode’s appeal: ordinary confidence meets a term that specialists know instantly and everyone else suddenly wishes they did.

episodes.title: Naked On Horseback
episodes.description: History becomes considerably less dignified when a famous naked horseback ride enters the quiz. The episode moves between respectable knowledge and wonderfully strange detail, demonstrating that education is apparently best retained when clothing is optional.

episodes.title: Quotidian
episodes.description: A deceptively ordinary word proves anything but quotidian as vocabulary becomes the episode’s defining curiosity. Language, culture and general knowledge mingle while a perfectly usable English word waits patiently to expose anyone who only half-remembers it.

episodes.title: Theodolite
episodes.description: Surveying equipment gets an unlikely moment of television glory with the theodolite. The episode is a celebration of Millionaire’s favourite trick: selecting some specialised object you have definitely seen, then demanding that you know what it is called.

seasons.description: Literature, supersonic aviation, animation, games, measurement, early aircraft, Scottish geography, wine country and ancient history drive a broad run of questions that rewards precise recall rather than comfortable familiarity.

episodes.title: White Chocolate
episodes.description: White chocolate provides the episode’s sweetest piece of trivia, though the question ladder itself is less forgiving. Food, culture and assorted general knowledge turn familiar things into precise distinctions, which is basically Millionaire’s preferred form of mischief.

episodes.title: The Count Of Monte Cristo
episodes.description: Dumas’s great tale of imprisonment and revenge supplies an appropriately dramatic title. Literature joins a broad question set where recognition comes easily, exact recall less so, and every confident memory seems to arrive carrying a small legal disclaimer.

episodes.title: Concorde
episodes.description: Concorde brings supersonic elegance to the question ladder. Aviation history gives the episode its sleekest subject while the quiz ranges elsewhere with rather less aerodynamic efficiency, forcing contestants to navigate facts at considerably below Mach 2.

episodes.title: Mufasa
episodes.description: Mufasa gives the episode a regal dose of animated familiarity. Popular culture sits comfortably beside more traditional quiz material, proving that Millionaire has no ideological objection to making childhood memories compete directly with serious general knowledge.

episodes.title: Solitaire
episodes.description: Solitaire becomes the episode’s neatly self-contained puzzle within a much larger puzzle. Games and everyday knowledge share space with broader trivia, and something normally associated with passing time suddenly acquires the gravity of a studio decision.

episodes.title: Nearest Whole Inch
episodes.description: ‘Nearest whole inch’ turns mundane measurement into an unexpectedly memorable phrase. The episode thrives on exactly that kind of precision: questions that seem harmless until a unit, definition or tiny wording choice becomes the entire problem.

episodes.title: The Sopwith Camel
episodes.description: The Sopwith Camel flies in from early aviation history, instantly giving the episode a wonderfully specific identity. Machines, history and general knowledge mix on a ladder where knowing that something existed is merely the opening bid.

episodes.title: Blaise Pascal
episodes.description: Blaise Pascal brings mathematics, philosophy and scientific history into a single name. The episode’s wider question set remains cheerfully eclectic, but Pascal supplies the kind of learned reference that makes Millionaire briefly resemble an exam nobody revised for.

episodes.title: The Isle Of Skye
episodes.description: The Isle of Skye provides a scenic pause in an otherwise unforgiving knowledge ladder. Scottish geography becomes the episode’s anchor while the questions roam elsewhere, because apparently even imaginary travel must be interrupted by multiple-choice uncertainty.

episodes.title: Colchagua Valley
episodes.description: Chile’s Colchagua Valley gives the episode a distinctly vinicultural detour. Geography and specialist knowledge meet in one elegant place-name, surrounded by the usual unpredictable shuffle of subjects that makes preparation for Millionaire essentially impossible.

episodes.title: Alexander The Great
episodes.description: Alexander the Great marches into the question set with considerably more confidence than most people bring to the hot seat. Ancient history supplies the episode’s headline figure while the rest of the ladder ranges across less conquerable territory.

seasons.description: Christmas and celebrity episodes open a run that moves through art, animation, astronomy, radioactivity, international institutions, Viennese food, classical music, Venice, cosmology and Roman history.

episodes.title: Young Boy Urinating
episodes.description: Art and public monuments reach one of their less dignified moments when a young boy urinating becomes legitimate quiz material. Christmas television rarely receives a more efficient reminder that Millionaire can make absolutely anything academically relevant.

episodes.title: Wallace And Gromit
episodes.description: Wallace and Gromit bring stop-motion charm to the question ladder, where even beloved animation is fair game for exact recall. The episode bounces between popular culture and broader trivia without allowing familiarity to become comfort.

episodes.title: Astronomical Distances
episodes.description: The scale of the universe becomes quiz material through astronomical distances. Cosmic numbers and earthly general knowledge share the same ladder, making the episode a neat demonstration that both the very large and the very trivial can be equally troublesome.

episodes.title: Radioactivity
episodes.description: Radioactivity gives the episode a scientific glow, strictly metaphorical and therefore considerably safer. Physics and general knowledge meet on a ladder where invisible phenomena are somehow easier to discuss than the visible four options on screen.

episodes.title: UNESCO
episodes.description: UNESCO turns an international acronym into the episode’s memorable knowledge checkpoint. Institutions, culture and assorted trivia share the ladder, with the familiar quiz-show lesson that recognising an abbreviation is not remotely the same as expanding it correctly.

episodes.title: Sachertorte
episodes.description: Vienna’s Sachertorte supplies a rich slice of culinary trivia. Food becomes serious business for a moment before the ladder moves elsewhere, leaving behind the useful discovery that cake knowledge can apparently sit comfortably beside history and science.

episodes.title: Eroica Symphony
episodes.description: Beethoven’s Eroica Symphony brings heroic musical ambition to the hot seat. Classical culture anchors an otherwise varied question set, and the episode briefly suggests civilisation is progressing before another multiple-choice dilemma restores normality.

episodes.title: Gondola
episodes.description: A Venetian gondola gives the episode a graceful visual centre. Travel, culture and ordinary knowledge drift through the ladder rather less serenely, because Millionaire remains one of the few places where a pleasant boat ride can become an exam question.

episodes.title: Stephen Hawking
episodes.description: Stephen Hawking lends the episode some formidable scientific gravity. Cosmology and popular knowledge meet in a broad ladder that reminds everyone how comforting famous names are right up until the question asks for one precise fact about them.

episodes.title: Crossing The Rubicon
episodes.description: Crossing the Rubicon supplies history, metaphor and irreversible decision-making in one useful phrase. It is almost suspiciously appropriate for Millionaire, where every answer eventually becomes its own tiny river with no convenient bridge back.

seasons.description: Geology, flooring, ancient landmarks, civil-rights history, zoology, ceremonial music and Fleet Street give this compact run an unusually varied path through science, culture, language and British history.

episodes.title: Igneous Rock
episodes.description: Igneous rock gives geology its turn under the studio lights. Earth science anchors a ladder of mixed knowledge where apparently solid facts can become surprisingly molten the moment four plausible alternatives are placed beside them.

episodes.title: Parquet
episodes.description: Parquet flooring becomes the episode’s beautifully ordinary piece of specialist vocabulary. Design, objects and general knowledge collide, proving once again that the most dangerous Millionaire questions are often about things people have walked over for years.

episodes.title: Pharos Of Alexandria
episodes.description: The Pharos of Alexandria lights up the episode with one of antiquity’s great landmarks. Ancient history stands tall among a roaming set of questions, even if the path to the correct answer is considerably less well illuminated.

episodes.title: I Have A Dream
episodes.description: One of history’s most recognisable phrases becomes the episode’s cultural landmark. Politics, history and general knowledge converge around ‘I Have a Dream’, while the ladder tests whether familiarity with famous words extends to the facts surrounding them.

episodes.title: Toothed Whale
episodes.description: A toothed whale swims into the question set as the episode’s natural-history oddity. Classification becomes unexpectedly consequential, and the ladder demonstrates that knowing an animal exists is merely the beginner level of quiz zoology.

episodes.title: Bridal Chorus
episodes.description: The Bridal Chorus gives the festive episode an unexpectedly matrimonial soundtrack. Music and ceremony join the usual knowledge mixture, with a tune almost everyone can recognise becoming much more interesting once recognition is no longer enough.

episodes.title: Fleet Street
episodes.description: Fleet Street brings newspapers, London history and cultural shorthand into the hot seat. The episode moves through a broad range of knowledge while one famous street demonstrates how geography can become an entire profession’s nickname.

seasons.description: New Zealand geography, Latin phrases, military aviation, geology, British food, volcanoes, folklore, literature, flight systems, urban history and engineering make this one of the revival’s widest-ranging stretches of general knowledge.

episodes.title: Cook Strait
episodes.description: Cook Strait places New Zealand geography squarely in the question ladder. Islands, waterways and general knowledge combine in an episode where knowing roughly where something is located proves less useful than knowing exactly what separates what.

episodes.title: Annus Horribilis
episodes.description: ‘Annus horribilis’ gives the episode a magnificent Latin phrase for a terrible year. Language and history mingle with the wider ladder, and two words manage to sound both scholarly and brutally efficient, an achievement most metadata can only envy.

episodes.title: Stratofortress
episodes.description: The B-52 Stratofortress lends the episode eight engines’ worth of Cold War presence. Aviation and military technology provide the standout machinery while the question set ranges elsewhere with considerably less predictable flight planning.

episodes.title: Hoodoos
episodes.description: Hoodoos give geology one of its stranger and more memorable words. The sculpted rock formations anchor an episode full of mixed trivia, demonstrating that Earth itself occasionally names things as though preparing material for a quiz show.

episodes.title: Melton Mowbray
episodes.description: Melton Mowbray turns a Leicestershire place-name into a distinctly edible piece of British knowledge. Geography, food and culture intersect before the ladder moves on, leaving everyone suddenly aware that regional specialities are dangerous quiz territory.

episodes.title: Mount Tambora
episodes.description: Mount Tambora brings volcanic history on a truly enormous scale. Geography and natural science give the episode its explosive centre while the surrounding questions prove that intellectual eruptions can occur without any assistance from magma.

episodes.title: Grim Reaper
episodes.description: The Grim Reaper stalks into an otherwise civilised general-knowledge quiz and immediately improves the iconography. Folklore and culture share the ladder with more ordinary subjects, making mortality briefly just another four-option problem.

episodes.title: Mario Puzo
episodes.description: Mario Puzo brings literary and cinematic crime history into the question set. A famous name sits amid broader trivia, with the episode testing the usual uncomfortable boundary between ‘I know exactly who that is’ and ‘I know one fact about him’.

episodes.title: Four Digit Transponder Code
episodes.description: A four-digit transponder code gives aviation terminology its wonderfully specific moment in the hot seat. The episode ranges through familiar and obscure knowledge while one compact sequence of numbers proves that even routine cockpit systems can become trivia.

episodes.title: Spitfire
episodes.description: The Spitfire gives the episode an unmistakable silhouette and a dose of aviation history. The ladder moves through other subjects, but few quiz answers arrive with quite so much cultural recognition packed into a single word.

episodes.title: The Iceberg Theory
episodes.description: The iceberg theory turns what lies beneath the surface into the episode’s central idea. Literature and interpretation join a broad question set, fittingly reminding contestants that the visible wording is not always the whole problem.

episodes.title: Kowloon Walled City
episodes.description: Kowloon Walled City supplies one of the catalogue’s most evocative place-names. Urban history and geography enter the ladder through a settlement famous for density and complexity, qualities the question set seems perfectly happy to imitate.

episodes.title: Aswan High Dam
episodes.description: The Aswan High Dam gives the episode monumental engineering on the Nile. Geography, infrastructure and history intersect in a ladder that keeps proving large human achievements are much easier to admire than to recall under four-answer pressure.

seasons.description: A short celebrity run moves through cycling, steam power, metallurgy, automotive vocabulary and science-fiction cinema, finding quiz-worthy specificity in subjects that range from everyday machinery to fictional spacecraft.

episodes.title: Peloton
episodes.description: Peloton turns a compact French-derived word into the episode’s sporting identifier. Cycling terminology joins the wider trivia mix, and something perfectly ordinary to enthusiasts becomes another specialised trap for everybody who merely owns a bicycle.

episodes.title: Steam Locomotive
episodes.description: The steam locomotive gives the episode a reassuringly mechanical centrepiece. Transport history meets general knowledge on a ladder where pistons and boilers are arguably simpler than the human process of choosing between four almost-plausible answers.

episodes.title: Stainless Steel
episodes.description: Stainless steel makes everyday material science unexpectedly quiz-worthy. Chemistry, invention and ordinary life converge around something encountered constantly but rarely considered, which is exactly the sort of neglected knowledge Millionaire enjoys weaponising.

episodes.title: Dipstick
episodes.description: The humble dipstick gets its improbable starring role. Automotive vocabulary anchors a mixed question set and demonstrates the show’s democratic approach to knowledge: emperors, equations and oily measuring rods are all equally capable of causing trouble.

episodes.title: Discovery One
episodes.description: Discovery One brings cinematic space travel into the question ladder with impeccable science-fiction pedigree. Film knowledge and broader trivia orbit one another in an episode where remembering a fictional spacecraft can become very real intellectual work.

seasons.description: Literature, ancient history, yoga, political history, biology, transport, Orwell, art, music and philosophy lead into later questions on airships, cryptozoology, geography and Shakespearean language within the same broadcaster season.

episodes.title: Paradise Lost
episodes.description: Milton’s Paradise Lost lends the episode biblical scale and literary weight. Poetry and culture sit among a roaming set of questions, though the title also rather neatly describes what happens to confidence whenever an unfamiliar option appears.

episodes.title: Babylon
episodes.description: Babylon brings the ancient world into the hot seat with one compact, resonant name. History and culture spread outward from it through a typically eclectic ladder, where several millennia of human knowledge are treated as reasonable revision material.

episodes.title: Downward Facing Dog
episodes.description: Yoga contributes the wonderfully literal Downward Facing Dog. The pose gives the episode an instantly visual identity while the ladder stretches across unrelated subjects, offering considerably less relaxation than the terminology might suggest.

episodes.title: Black Power
episodes.description: ‘Black Power’ gives the episode a charged piece of twentieth-century political and cultural history. The question ladder moves through broader knowledge while one short phrase carries far more historical context than its two words initially reveal.

episodes.title: Parthenogenesis
episodes.description: Parthenogenesis gives biology one of the catalogue’s finest technical words. Reproduction without fertilisation becomes legitimate prime-time trivia, surrounded by a question set that makes ordinary human memory feel unnecessarily complicated by comparison.

episodes.title: Grand Central Station
episodes.description: Grand Central Station brings New York scale and railway grandeur into the episode. Architecture, transport and cultural geography meet a wider ladder that makes one of the world’s busiest terminals seem almost calm by comparison.

episodes.title: Room 101
episodes.description: Room 101 turns Orwellian dread into an unusually tidy episode title. Literature and popular culture merge around a phrase that escaped its novel and entered everyday language, exactly the kind of transformation quiz writers adore.

episodes.title: Canaletto
episodes.description: Canaletto gives Venetian art a crisp single-name identity on the ladder. Painting and cultural history join the wider trivia mix, with the episode asking viewers to distinguish genuine familiarity from that dangerous museum-grade feeling of ‘I’ve seen this somewhere’.

episodes.title: O Sole Mio
episodes.description: ‘O Sole Mio’ brings one of Italy’s most recognisable melodies into the quiz. Music and cultural knowledge share the episode with unrelated trivia, proving a tune can be instantly familiar while every factual detail around it remains negotiable.

episodes.title: Hell Is Other People
episodes.description: Sartre contributes the gloriously cheerful observation that hell is other people. Philosophy and literature give the episode a memorable sting while the rest of the ladder offers its own less existential but equally effective forms of discomfort.

episodes.title: The Hindenburg
episodes.description: The Hindenburg brings airship history and catastrophe into the question set with unavoidable dramatic weight. The rest of the ladder ranges more quietly, but few subjects can match a giant zeppelin for immediate visual identity.

episodes.title: Patterson-Gimlin Film
episodes.description: The Patterson-Gimlin film drags Bigfoot into the respectable surroundings of a prime-time quiz. Cryptozoology and cultural history make a wonderfully strange stop on a ladder otherwise pretending that human knowledge has sensible boundaries.

episodes.title: Tango And Tonga
episodes.description: Tango and Tonga form a pleasingly improbable pair in the episode’s standout question. Similar sounds, very different meanings, and exactly the sort of linguistic-geographical collision that makes multiple choice feel less helpful than advertised.

episodes.title: Method In My Madness
episodes.description: ‘Method in my madness’ gives the episode a Shakespearean phrase with suspicious relevance to quiz strategy. Language and culture mingle with the wider ladder while apparently chaotic thinking occasionally reveals a plan underneath.

seasons.description: Renaissance art, Greek mythology, opera, astronomy, medicine, deep time, architecture, literature, stamp design and Welsh geography define a run built around highly recognisable subjects that become much less comfortable under exact questioning.

episodes.title: Donatello
episodes.description: Donatello brings Renaissance sculpture into the hot seat, with several centuries of artistic reputation compressed into one answer. The episode’s broader trivia makes a familiar name compete against the awkward requirement of knowing exactly why it is familiar.

episodes.title: Cerberus
episodes.description: Cerberus guards the episode with three heads and excellent branding. Greek mythology provides the standout creature while the wider ladder ranges through science, language and culture, none of which comes with a convenient mythological watchdog.

episodes.title: Sull'aria
episodes.description: ‘Sull’aria’ gives the episode an elegant operatic identity. Classical music enters the ladder through a phrase more likely to be sung than spoken, surrounded by the usual Millionaire mixture of knowledge that refuses to stay in one key.

episodes.title: The Bringer Of Peace
episodes.description: ‘The Bringer of Peace’ lends the episode a grand musical and astronomical flavour without needing the planet’s name in the title. The phrase hangs memorably above a ladder that is considerably less peaceful for anyone answering it.

episodes.title: Digitalis
episodes.description: Digitalis gives botany and medicine a beautifully precise shared word. A plant-derived term becomes the episode’s defining curiosity while the rest of the ladder demonstrates how quickly familiar-looking scientific vocabulary can become hostile.

episodes.title: Paleozoic
episodes.description: The Paleozoic era stretches the episode’s timeline back hundreds of millions of years. Deep time joins contemporary general knowledge on the same ladder, making the difference between ancient geology and yesterday’s trivia feel almost administratively small.

episodes.title: Bellatrix
episodes.description: Bellatrix supplies a name shared by astronomy and modern popular imagination. The episode exploits exactly that sort of layered familiarity, moving through a question set where recognition is abundant but precise context remains stubbornly rationed.

episodes.title: Gargoyle
episodes.description: A gargoyle peers down from the episode’s architectural trivia with the appropriate amount of menace. Buildings, culture and general knowledge mingle on a ladder where decorative stonework is somehow permitted to judge people back.

episodes.title: Ulysses
episodes.description: Ulysses brings an ancient hero, a literary landmark and a famously overloaded name into the quiz. The episode’s wider questions continue the theme of making apparently familiar references much less comfortable when context suddenly matters.

episodes.title: Machin Series
episodes.description: The Machin Series turns an everyday piece of British visual design into specialised trivia. It is the sort of object millions have encountered without naming, making it almost perfectly engineered for Millionaire’s particular strain of annoyance.

episodes.title: Red Wharf Bay
episodes.description: Red Wharf Bay gives the episode a striking piece of Welsh geography. A place-name with instant atmosphere anchors a broad ladder, where knowing Britain well still leaves plenty of room for one coastline to become surprisingly consequential.

seasons.description: Astronomy, Latin, architecture, robotics, Apollo history, science fiction, classical music, orbital mechanics, Elizabethan conspiracy, neuroscience and language carry the quiz from early 2025 into the first months of 2026.

episodes.title: Scintillation
episodes.description: Scintillation explains why stars appear to twinkle and gives the episode a beautifully technical title. Astronomy turns a familiar night-sky observation into precise science, while the rest of the ladder performs its own less attractive flickering of certainty.

episodes.title: Pro Bono
episodes.description: ‘Pro bono’ brings compact Latin into everyday professional language and the question ladder. The episode makes familiar phrases feel newly examinable, because apparently using an expression for years is no guarantee of knowing exactly what it means.

episodes.title: Portmeirion
episodes.description: Portmeirion provides architecture, Wales and a touch of surreal visual character in one memorable place. The episode wanders through broader knowledge, but a village that already looks slightly improbable is ideally suited to becoming quiz trivia.

episodes.title: Eden Project
episodes.description: The Eden Project brings giant biomes and ambitious environmental design into the hot seat. Architecture, science and geography meet on a ladder where an enormous greenhouse complex is somehow among the easier things to visualise.

episodes.title: End Effector
episodes.description: ‘End effector’ gives robotics a term that sounds vaguely ominous until it is explained. Engineering supplies the episode’s best piece of specialist vocabulary, surrounded by questions that make the human answering mechanism look comparatively unreliable.

episodes.title: Lunar Module Eagle
episodes.description: Lunar Module Eagle lands in the episode with one of space exploration’s most recognisable machine names. Apollo-era history anchors a broad ladder where remembering humanity’s giant leaps still depends on several very small factual steps.

episodes.title: Arthur Dent
episodes.description: Arthur Dent brings bathrobes, bureaucracy and cosmic inconvenience into the question set. Science fiction supplies the episode’s most personable reference while the wider ladder remains almost as indifferent to human comfort as the universe he inhabits.

episodes.title: Also Sprach Zarathustra
episodes.description: ‘Also Sprach Zarathustra’ gives the episode a monumental musical title familiar far beyond the concert hall. Classical culture meets cinema and general knowledge, with a piece everyone recognises proving rather fewer people can confidently name.

episodes.title: Perturbation
episodes.description: Perturbation turns orbital mechanics into one elegant scientific headache. Gravitational influence gives the episode its technical centre while the wider ladder repeatedly perturbs contestants’ own trajectories away from comfortable certainty.

episodes.title: The Babington Plot
episodes.description: The Babington Plot brings Elizabethan espionage and conspiracy into the hot seat. Codes, intrigue and political history give the episode narrative energy, while the surrounding ladder reminds us that treason is easier to follow with multiple-choice options.

episodes.title: The Hypothalamus
episodes.description: The hypothalamus gives neuroscience its compact starring role. A tiny region of the brain becomes a large quiz concern, surrounded by a ladder that would be much easier if the organ being tested came with a built-in answer key.

episodes.title: Serendipity
episodes.description: Serendipity gives the episode a word for fortunate accidental discovery. It is a charming concept for a quiz where success occasionally resembles exactly that, although the ladder continues to insist on calling it knowledge.

episodes.title: Precognition
episodes.description: Precognition brings knowledge of the future into a programme devoted to proving how unreliable knowledge of the present can be. The paranormal concept gives the episode a neat identity while the ladder remains stubbornly resistant to prophecy.

episodes.title: Ornithopter
episodes.description: The ornithopter gives flight a wonderfully mechanical imitation of birds. Engineering and imagination meet in one distinctive word, while the episode’s broader questions demonstrate that humans can copy wings more readily than they can organise memory.

episodes.title: Velociraptor
episodes.description: Velociraptor brings prehistoric speed and pop-cultural menace into the quiz. Paleontology supplies an instantly recognisable creature, though the episode still finds ways to make familiarity with dinosaurs less useful than childhood enthusiasm promised.

episodes.title: Frangipane
episodes.description: Frangipane gives the episode almond-filled culinary precision. Baking terminology becomes serious quiz business for a moment, proving that pastry knowledge can stand beside science, history and literature without displaying the slightest inferiority complex.

episodes.title: The Moons Of Uranus
episodes.description: The moons of Uranus send the episode into the outer Solar System. Astronomy provides a wonderfully named family of worlds while the question ladder makes planetary distances seem simple compared with retrieving the correct fact from memory.

seasons.description: A Christmas journey on the Orient Express leads into 2026 questions on mythology, theatre, horror, Scottish history and other eclectic subjects as Clarkson continues putting six contestants at a time through the Millionaire chair.

episodes.title: Orient Express
episodes.description: The Orient Express carries the Christmas episode into a world of luxury rail travel and cultural legend. The question set ranges elsewhere, but few names can match a famous train for combining geography, history and instant atmosphere.

episodes.title: Theatre Of The Absurd
episodes.description: The Theatre of the Absurd lends the episode a cultural label that could occasionally describe quiz television itself. Drama and philosophy meet a varied ladder where logic remains available, merely not always at the moment it would be useful.

episodes.title: Cassandra
episodes.description: Cassandra brings the curse of true prophecy and universal disbelief into the hot seat. Greek mythology supplies a concept almost cruelly suited to multiple choice: being right is useful only if you can persuade yourself to trust it.

episodes.title: Overlook Hotel
episodes.description: The Overlook Hotel checks horror cinema into the question ladder with suitably ominous hospitality. Film knowledge gives the episode its memorable location while the surrounding trivia offers plenty of other corridors in which certainty can get lost.

episodes.title: Medusa
episodes.description: Medusa brings snakes, stone and one of mythology’s most recognisable faces into the quiz. Ancient legend supplies the episode’s visual centre while the ladder sensibly avoids making eye contact and moves on to other forms of danger.

episodes.title: Caledonia
episodes.description: Caledonia gives Scotland its poetic old name and the episode a compact historical identity. Geography, language and culture converge around a word that sounds familiar long before most people are asked to define it precisely.
